# Title

Computational design of light and strong high entropy alloys (HEA): Obtainment of an extremely high specific solid solution hardening

# Authors

Edern Menou, Franck Tancret, Isaac Toda-Caraballo, Gérard Ramstein, Philippe Castany, Emmanuel Bertrand, Nicolas Gautier, Pedro Eduardo Jose Rivera Díaz-Del-Castillo

## Abstract

A multi-objective optimisation genetic algorithm combining solid solution hardening (SSH) and thermodynamic modelling (CALPHAD) with data mining is used to design high entropy alloys (HEAs). The approach searches for the best compromise between single-phase stability, SSH and density. Thousands of Pareto-optimal base-centred cubic (BCC) HEAs are designed. Al35Cr35Mn8Mo5Ti17 (at.%) is chosen for experimental validation. The alloy was cast and characterised. Its microstructure consists of large grains of a single disordered solid solution displaying a Vickers hardness of 6.45 GPa (658 HV) and a density below 5.5 g/cm3; uniquely combining exceptional hardness with medium density.

# Introduction

The maximisation of specific strength is a major driving force for engineering materials design and selection [1]. In engineering alloys high hardness is typically achieved either in ordered intermetallic compounds, in which atoms of different nature are localised on different lattice sites, or as a result of mechanisms such as solid solution, grain refinement, strain and precipitation hardening. Solid solution hardening (SSH) results from alloying additions leading to variations in atom spacing; this is thought to increase the energy required for dislocation glide [2,3]. The case of so-called high entropy alloys (HEAs) [4,5] is of particular interest when considering SSH as they are highly concentrated multicomponent systems. HEAs may exhibit SSH well beyond the levels found in conventional alloys, as the consequence of being highly concentrated solid solutions of different elements, hence cumulating several contributions of atoms with large size differences [6,7]. However, although such atomic size dissimilarity increases the SSH effect, Hume-Rothery rules dictate that atomic species of dissimilar size would likely lead to phase decomposition. A challenge for HEA design is therefore to maximise SSH due to the high elemental concentration whilst preventing the formation of a product phase. This work provides a new computational method to maximise SSH whilst preventing phase decomposition in low-density alloys.

In the search for alloys combining high mechanical properties and a low density, the possibility to obtain HEAs incorporating light elements may pave the way to fabricate light and strong alloys relying on SSH. The development of HEAs has so far mainly relied on trial-and-error experiments guided by a set of physicochemical rules [8–14] and on modelling [15–17]. This has provided individual predictions or even methods to explore certain alloy systems systematically [18,19] or in a guided manner [20]. More recently, an integrated computational alloy design strategy was implemented to identify new face-centred cubic (FCC) HEAs with advantageous combinations of strength and density, using a genetic algorithm multi-objective optimisation method relying on various models to predict alloy characteristics (density, SSH and solid solution stability) [21]. Notably, a new FCC HEA has been designed, possessing unique combinations of mechanical properties and density compared to other annealed large grain HEAs. Nevertheless, SSH in most FCC HEAs remains modest with a yield stress of the order of 200 MPa [22], whereas densities well below those of most FCC HEAs (typically around 8 g/cm3) seem unreachable. In contrast with FCC systems, base-centred cubic (BCC) HEAs may offer much higher levels of SSH and significantly lower densities [22]. The present work focuses on the computational design of light and strong BCC HEAs, and the experimental verification of the associated models.

# Methods/Experimental

The adopted alloy design strategy involves a multi-objective optimisation algorithm, based on the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm, version II (NSGA-II) [23]. The algorithm was adapted to account for the high-dimensionality and constrained nature of alloy design [24], and conforms to the combinatorial requirements of HEAs design [21]. Such modified algorithm was employed to optimise alloy density, strength and phase stability as a function of composition. The essential features of the approach included:

- A statistics-based criterion, PIF, to estimate the probability of forming a single solid solution, obtained by data mining complemented by computational thermodynamics using the CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) method [21,25,26].
- The prediction of crystal structure using the valence electron concentration, VEC [13].
- A rule of mixtures to estimate density.
- A physical model to predict the SSH of multi-elemental highly-concentrated alloys [6,7].

According to the most widely accepted definition, HEAs are made of at least five different elements, each concentrated between 5 at.% and 35 at.% [27]. The design space covered alloys containing five or more elements among a palette of sixteen (Al, Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Hf, Mn, Mo, Nb, Ni, Ru, Ta, Ti, V, W and Zr), making a total of \(\sum_{n=5}^{16} \binom{16}{n} = 63019\) possible families of alloys. Elemental concentrations could be either zero or between 5 and 35 at.% in steps of 1 at.%, corresponding potentially to trillions of different alloys. Multi-objective optimisation was run with the aim of maximising the probability to form BCC HEAs, maximising their SSH and minimising their density, while the minimum number of elements in the alloys was set to five. The optimisation was run fifty times with different initialisations of random numbers used by the genetic algorithm, to check that similar results were produced. The total calculation took approximately one hundred hours on a single-node computer during which about eight million alloys were evaluated, which corresponds to enough evaluations for a GA to guarantee convergence to the optimum [28]. The genetic algorithm produced 3155 alloys that are Pareto-optimal or non-dominated, meaning that, for each of them, no other alloy exists that would simultaneously have a higher probability to form a single solid solution, a higher SSH and a lower density. Results are plotted on Fig. 1.

Interestingly, this Pareto set reflects the antagonistic nature of two of the objectives, namely SSH and solid-solution stability. For a given level of density, alloys with the highest predicted SSH are mostly associated to the lowest probabilities of forming a single solid solution, which is consistent with Hume-Rothery rules. This result highlights the usefulness of multi-objective optimisation to discover the best possible trade-off between phase stability and SSH. All three objectives span over wide ranges (see Fig. 1). Pareto-optimal alloys belong to 59 different alloy families, representing only ~0.09% of the 63,019 possible ones; all of them contain either five, six or seven elements. The first ten most frequent families in terms of number of alloys are listed in Table 1; they represent 60% of all designed alloys. It is worth noting the novelty of these families with respect to the existing HEAs reported in the literature (see for instance [22]). Only one family in Table 1, MoNbTaTiVW, has already been reported, although it was at equimolar composition [29]. It is also close to the classic alloy MoNbTaVW, also BCC [30] and its sub-systems [31]. Just two other families in Table 1, MoNbTiWZr and MoNbTiVWZr, have some similarities with an existing alloy, MoNbTiVZr [32], reported as BCC, although they are different families if strictly considering the lists of elements. All other families differ from existing ones by at least two elements.

Aluminium and chromium are the most frequently found elements resulting from the optimisation; each is present with a concentration of 35 at.% in more than 40% of alloys. Conversely, nickel, copper and ruthenium are never present, and some elements are rarely found: cobalt and hafnium are present only at 5 at.% concentration, in ~0.2% and in ~2% of alloys, respectively, while iron is part of ~8% of alloys (with ~6% containing only 5 at.% of Fe). Other elements display an intermediate frequency.

An interesting fact is that the Pareto set contains no equiatomic alloy. Although equimolarity was initially considered to favour the stability of HEAs and to confer them a high SSH [27], it was already recognised that configurational entropy was not a major feature triggering the formation of a single solid solution [26]; this is confirmed here. Actually, it seems that the algorithm pushed compositions as far as possible away from equimolarity; this is evidenced by calculating the average deviation (AD) from equimolar compositions as:

\[
AD = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left|x_i - \frac{1}{n}\right|
\]

where \(n\) is the number of elements in the alloy and \(x_i\) is the atomic fraction of element \(i\); this quantity would be null for an equimolar alloy. However, among the designed HEAs, no alloy exhibits AD under 6 at.%, whereas 72% of alloys feature an AD around 12 at.%, which is close to the maximum possible value for HEAs of five, six or seven elements.

It is worth noting that some of the obtained features are similar to those found in the design of FCC HEAs [21]. These include a compromise between SSH and density, number of optimal alloys (several thousands), number of families (a few tens), ten families representing the majority of alloys, absence of equiatomic alloys and a generally high AD.

Among the 3155 Pareto-optimal alloys one has been selected for experimental validation. The chosen alloy displayed the highest specific SSH. The potential of the chosen material to be a HEA was cross-checked by computational thermodynamics using the CALPHAD software Thermo-Calc [33], by ensuring that four thermodynamic databases (TTNI8 [34], TCNI7 [33], TCFE8 [33] and SSOL5 [35]) would predict the stability of a single solid solution at least at one temperature over the range 700 °C–1300 °C. These criteria led to alloy Al35Cr35Mn8Mo5Ti17 (at.%) which has not been reported so far. Moreover, to the author's knowledge, the AlCrMnMoTi system has not yet been reported in the literature to form HEAs. According to predictions, this alloy would have a SSH of 1316 MPa for a density of 5.10 g/cm3.

The chosen alloy was fabricated by vacuum arc melting as a bar of approximately 12 mm in diameter and 100 mm in length. After determining an appropriate heat treatment temperature using Thermo-Calc, the alloy was homogenised for 24 h at 1300 °C under vacuum and water-quenched.

The specimen was ground to mirror polishing for Field Emission Gun Scanning Electron Microscope (FEG-SEM) observation. Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) analysis, conducted under 20 kV in the FEG-SEM, indicated an actual composition of Al31Cr37Mn7Mo6Ti19 (at.%), whereas the nominal composition is Al35Cr35Mn8Mo5Ti17 (at.%). EDS mapping evidenced the absence of atomic contrast. No contrast was obtained at any scale using back-scattered electrons (BSE). Sample preparation using vibratory polishing in silica suspension for 12 h was then employed in order to observe the microstructure. Fig. 2a shows very large grains revealed by crystallographic contrast.

Phase constitution was characterised by X-ray diffraction, XRD (employing copper Kα radiation). As the grains are very large, the alloy is mechanically milled into a fine powder to increase the number of diffracting crystallites. The diffraction pattern (Fig. 2b), recorded with 2θ from 20° to 90°, only displays fine peaks of a single BCC solid solution: (110), (200) and (211). Bragg's law yields a lattice parameter value of 0.304 nm, corresponding to a density of 5.48 g/cm3 using the composition obtained by EDS, and 5.33 g/cm3 with nominal composition. Density was also measured by a balance density determination kit; a value of 5.32 g/cm3 was found. The predicted value being 5.10 g/cm3, the agreement is rather fair.

Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) was used to characterise the alloy at finer scales to confirm its single phase nature and the absence of, for instance, nano-sized precipitates, local ordering or twins. A Jeol 2100 LaB6-gun TEM machine working at a 200 kV accelerating voltage was used. A bright field image is shown on Fig. 3a. Only a single crystal is visible with few dislocations and without any evidence of precipitates. A selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern of the same grain is displayed in Fig. 3b. Only spots related to a BCC phase along a 〈100〉 zone axis can be observed with neither additional reflections that would indicate the presence of precipitates even at nanometric scale, nor streaks, evidencing the sole presence of a disordered solid solution. The reciprocal distances between spots are in good agreement with the lattice parameter of 0.304 nm determined by XRD.

# Results

Considering the results obtained by XRD, by SEM at all reachable scales both in the SE and BSE modes, by EDS and by TEM including imaging and electron diffraction, there is no doubt that the new material is actually constituted of a single disordered BCC solid solution.

Vickers hardness was determined under a load of 0.5 kg (4.9 N) and averaged over ten measurements. A mean value of 6.45 GPa (658 HV) was obtained. The new material is a single disordered solid solution, with large grains, i.e. without any significant Hall-Petch effect, and was annealed at a high temperature so that any possible strain hardening effect has vanished (which is also evidenced by the very fine XRD peaks), so that the high hardness measured must originate only from the solid solution contribution. Fig. 4 presents a hardness-density chart, where the new alloy is compared to other BCC HEAs [36–42], showing its superiority.

To the best of authors' knowledge, the designed material presents the highest substitutional solid solution hardening ever obtained in any metallic alloy. This is achieved in a material with a density of less than 5.5 g/cm3, so that the designed material is one of the hardest known metallic alloys for such low density.

# Discussion

The Pareto set reflects the antagonistic relation between solid solution hardening and single-phase stability, consistent with Hume-Rothery rules. The multi-objective framework was necessary to identify compositions that best balance these opposing tendencies while also minimizing density. The resulting design space contained more than 3000 Pareto-optimal compositions predicted to be BCC HEAs. The absence of equiatomic alloys among the optimal solutions further supports the view that configurational entropy alone is not the dominant factor governing single-solid-solution formation in these systems.

The experimentally selected alloy, Al35Cr35Mn8Mo5Ti17, reached an actual composition of Al31Cr37Mn7Mo6Ti19 after casting and processing, yet still formed a single disordered BCC solid solution with large grains and no evidence of precipitates, local ordering, twins, or strain hardening. Its hardness of 6.45 GPa (658 HV) together with density below 5.5 g/cm3 places it in a distinct region of the hardness-density space compared with previously reported BCC HEAs.

# Conclusions

To summarise, we conducted the computational design of light and strong HEAs by associating a probabilistic model obtained by data mining of physico-chemical parameters to predict solid solution stability [21,25], CALPHAD [25], physical models to predict the SSH contribution [6,7] and crystal structure [13] of multiconcentrated alloys, the prediction of density using a rule of mixtures, and a multi-objective optimisation genetic algorithm specifically adapted to HEAs [21]. This was made to tackle the compromise between solid solution hardening and single-phase stability. In this respect, the genetic algorithm optimised compositions such as to find the best possible trade-off between both within a multi-objective frame. The latter was also implemented in the search for the best possible compromise between two other usually conflicting properties, the strength and density. In fact, the three characteristics were optimised simultaneously, which led to the design of more than 3000 compositions, for which the physico-chemical and thermodynamic calculations predicted to be BCC HEAs, being Pareto-optimal in terms of calculated stability, SSH and density. An alloy with nominal composition Al35Cr35Mn8Mo5Ti17 (at.%) was selected and fabricated, reaching an actual composition Al31Cr37Mn7Mo6Ti19 (at.%). It was then heat treated and fully characterised down to the nanometre scale, confirming it as a single BCC disordered solid solution, with large grains and no strain hardening. A Vickers hardness of 6.45 GPa (658 HV) and a density below 5.5 g/cm3 were obtained, exhibiting an exceptional solid solution hardening, and being one of the hardest metals ever recorded for such low density. Computational design combining physical models with data mining was the only way to discover such an alloy; experimental trial-and-error approaches would be unfeasible due the size of the composition space.
